1.pericope_label: The burden of Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite. God is jealous, and the Lord revengeth; the Lord revengeth, and is furious; the Lord will take vengeance on his adversaries, and he reserveth wrath for his enemies.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch gloss the prophet's name as consolation and argue a negative about his birthplace, denying the identification with a village east of the Tigris, and they read the opening description of God as having a double object, connecting the coming destruction of the Assyrian capital with the divine purpose at large. Ellicott renders the title simply as the sentence against Nineveh, refers the birthplace question to his introduction, and renders the opening as a jealous and vengeful God is Jehovah, an avenger, aye, wrathful.

Gill divides the divine jealousy in two, for God's own honour and worship, so that idolaters must be punished, and for his people, whose injuries he cannot bear to see unavenged; he also reports the Jewish tradition that the earlier prophet was rightly said to have prophesied against this city. Calvin derives the word rendered burden from the verb to bear, says the prophets used it whenever they denounced grievous vengeance, and adds that because it was so often threatened against the Jews the people came to call all prophecy by that name in ridicule.

Clarke glosses the terms of the opening description one by one and dwells on the last, that though such men seem to prosper for a time and God appears to have passed their crimes by, he reserves and treasures up wrath which will burst forth in due time. Wesley states the usage of the title plainly, that a burden was denounced against a nation or city, draws the prophet's name against his subject so that the comfort is Israel's and the burden Nineveh's, and grounds the vengeance in office rather than temper, since the supreme governor is bound to right the oppressed.

Henry presses the metaphor of the burden hardest, calling this not only a prophecy and a weighty one but a burdensome prophecy, a dead weight to the city and a millstone hung about its neck; and he dates the interval from the earlier preaching at about a hundred years, making the contrast that the overthrow then foretold was suspended when the Ninevites repented and were spared.

debates.question: What does the word rendered burden signify, and what force does it carry here?

positions.position: A denunciation of grievous vengeance, so often threatened that the people came to use the word of all prophecy in ridicule.
The standing technical usage: when prophets were sent to denounce judgments against a place, the word was called the burden of that place.
Simply the sentence against Nineveh, without pressing the metaphor.
A burdensome prophecy in the full weight of the figure, a dead weight and a millstone about the city's neck.

debates.question: Can the prophet's birthplace be located?

positions.position: Not in Assyria; the village east of the Tigris north-west of Khorsabad, two days from Mosul, is not the place.
The question is referred to the introduction and not settled here.

outliers.claim: The model the prophet is following in the opening description is a passage of opposite purport, the well-known proclamation of the divine attribute of mercy, which he is here deliberately reshaping.

themes: The burden of Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite.
God is jealous, and the Lord revengeth; the Lord revengeth, and is furious; the Lord will take vengeance on his adversaries, and he reserveth wrath for his enemies.

3.pericope_label: The Lord is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the Lord hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet. He rebuketh the sea, and maketh it dry, and drieth up all the rivers: Bashan languisheth, and Carmel, and the flower of Lebanon languisheth.

schools.summary: Ellicott turns on a single conjunction, reading that the Lord is slow to anger yet great in power, since the point is that his forbearance is not attributable to weakness; and he is the boldest of the four in tracing the storm imagery to the wonders of the exodus, the pillars of cloud and fire, the quaking mount, the sea and river divided and Canaan giving way. Keil and Delitzsch render the catalogue in their own version, that he threatens the sea and dries it up and makes all the rivers fail.

Gill puts the divine forbearance into the history of this particular city, which had already had proof of it when it repented at the earlier preaching and the wrath was deferred, and warns that they must not presume upon it now that they have returned to their former impieties. Calvin is the most guarded of the four on the exodus allusion: there may be an allusion to the history described by Moses, since the prophets often remind the people how their fathers were brought out of Egypt, and as that passage through the sea was held in high repute it may be that this prophet alludes to it.

Clarke states the forbearance without Ellicott's contrast, that God exercises much longsuffering toward his enemies so that it may lead them to repentance, and sums up the effect of the whole theophany rather than its source, calling the coming of God dreadfully majestic since he is represented as controlling universal nature. Wesley picks out the flower of the northern mountain as whatever flourished on it, and turns the strangest phrase in the passage into a military picture, the clouds being the dust of God's feet as an army far off is discovered by the dust it raises.

debates.question: How should the clause about power be construed against the clause about forbearance?

positions.position: Adversatively: slow to anger yet great in power, the forbearance not being attributable to weakness.
Without the contrast: the longsuffering is toward enemies that it may lead them to repentance, and the power is simply the ability at all times to save or destroy.

debates.question: Is the storm imagery drawn from the exodus?

positions.position: Yes, and explicitly: the prophet reverts in the manner of other Hebrew poets to the wonders of the desert march and the divided sea.
Possibly, and only possibly, since the prophets often recall the deliverance from Egypt and that passage was held in high repute.
The effect of the description matters more than its source, which is the control of universal nature.

outliers.claim: The clouds are the dust of God's feet, and though he is surrounded with darkness an army far off is nevertheless discovered by the dust its feet raise, so God appears with great power marching against his enemies.

themes: The Lord is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the Lord hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet.
He rebuketh the sea, and maketh it dry, and drieth up all the rivers: Bashan languisheth, and Carmel, and the flower of Lebanon languisheth.

5.pericope_label: The mountains quake at him, and the hills melt, and the earth is burned at his presence, yea, the world, and all that dwell therein. Who can stand before his indignation? and who can abide in the fierceness of his anger? his fury is poured out like fire, and the rocks are thrown down by him. The Lord is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him. But with an overrunning flood he will make an utter end of the place thereof, and darkness shall pursue his enemies.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch render the catalogue plainly, the mountains quaking, the hills melting and the earth heaving at his presence with the world and all that dwell in it. Ellicott corrects one word of the received version to the same effect, preferring heaves to is burned, and at the eighth verse changes a conjunction again, preferring and to but on the ground that God protects his afflicted servants and therefore exterminates their oppressor, so that the two clauses are one movement; he renders the last clause that he shall drive his enemies into darkness.

Gill takes the quaking mountains figuratively, reporting that mountains signify kings and princes and hills large countries, so that what trembles is the several kingdoms of the Assyrian empire; he answers the question of who can stand flatly, that no creature can, neither Nineveh nor the whole empire, and grounds the mercy of the seventh verse historically in the deliverance of Hezekiah. Calvin explains what the terrible description is for, that men might know none will stand at God's tribunal unless supported by his own favour, the enemies of the church being set before an account they must render.

Clarke says in his own idiom that in the midst of judgment God remembers mercy and mingles promises among the most dreadful denunciations of wrath, so that none who trust in him need be alarmed; and he offers a literal candidate for the flood image, reporting from an ancient historian that the river overflowed its banks, deluged part of the city and overturned twenty stadia of the wall. Wesley glosses the knowing of them as approving, owning and preserving them, and reads the flood as the figure of a river overflowing all its banks.

debates.question: Are the quaking mountains the hills themselves or the powers they stand for?

positions.position: Figurative: mountains are kings and princes, hills large countries, so the kingdoms of the empire tremble.
Rendered plainly as the physical catalogue, with heaves preferred to is burned.

debates.question: How does the eighth verse stand to the mercy that precedes it?

positions.position: As one continuous movement: read and, since God protects his servants and therefore exterminates their oppressor.
Adversatively: the flood is the judgment overwhelming Assyria, by a powerful army or under the figure of an overflowing river.

outliers.claim: Reports from an ancient historian, on a bishop's suggestion, that the river overflowed its banks, deluged part of the city and overturned twenty stadia of the wall, whereupon the despairing king burnt himself and his palace with his treasures.

themes: The mountains quake at him, and the hills melt, and the earth is burned at his presence, yea, the world, and all that dwell therein.
Who can stand before his indignation? and who can abide in the fierceness of his anger? his fury is poured out like fire, and the rocks are thrown down by him.
The Lord is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him.
But with an overrunning flood he will make an utter end of the place thereof, and darkness shall pursue his enemies.

9.pericope_label: What do ye imagine against the Lord? he will make an utter end: affliction shall not rise up the second time. For while they be folden together as thorns, and while they are drunken as drunkards, they shall be devoured as stubble fully dry.

schools.summary: Ellicott argues from the vocabulary that the affliction which shall not rise a second time is Nineveh's affliction of Israel, the same term used a few verses earlier for the trouble that came from Nineveh, and names the reading he rejects; he re-renders the similes of the next verse as bundles of thorn faggots and, even while steeped in their drink, stubble fully dry, explaining that dry thorn cuttings were commonly used as fuel. Keil and Delitzsch render the sequence without comment and carry it straight on to the wicked counsellor named next.

Gill reads the opening question as addressed to the enemy and answers it for them, asking whether they think they can frustrate God's designs, resist his power and hinder what he has determined; on the similes he keeps closest to the imagery of worthlessness, that they are like thorns useless and unprofitable, fit only for burning and, being bundled together, already prepared for it. Calvin reports a third construction of the disputed clause, that some understand it of the chosen people's own calamity, which would not be a destruction because God would keep within limits.

Clarke takes the clause of the judgment itself, that there will be no need to repeat it since with one blow God will make a full end of the business, and takes the folding quite differently from the others, not of a faggot but of counsel: however united their counsels may be, they shall be as drunken men, perplexed and unsteady in all their resolutions. Wesley makes the identification explicit, that what they imagine against God's people they imagine against him, and draws out that thorns bound together burn together and so help to destroy each other.

Henry places the whole passage historically, taking these verses to point at the destruction of the Assyrian army under Sennacherib, which he reckons a part of the burden of Nineveh and a pledge of the destruction of the city itself about a hundred years later, and noting that the prophet with whom this one was probably contemporary spoke much of that event.

debates.question: Whose affliction is it that shall not rise a second time?

positions.position: Nineveh's affliction of Israel: the same word is used earlier of the trouble that came from Nineveh, so the promise is that she shall not afflict Israel again.
The judgment itself: there is no need to repeat it, since with one blow God makes a full end.
A third construction is reported, that some understand it of the chosen people's own calamity, kept within limits and therefore not a destruction.

debates.question: What do the folded thorns and the drunkenness signify?

positions.position: Fuel: a compact bundle of dry thorn faggots and a second equally combustible material.
Mutual destruction: thorns bound together burn together, and the drunken are unable to help themselves.
United counsels: however united, they shall be as drunken men, perplexed and unsteady in all their resolutions.
Worthlessness: useless and pernicious, fit only for burning and already bundled for it.

themes: What do ye imagine against the Lord? he will make an utter end: affliction shall not rise up the second time.
For while they be folden together as thorns, and while they are drunken as drunkards, they shall be devoured as stubble fully dry.

11.pericope_label: There is one come out of thee, that imagineth evil against the Lord, a wicked counsellor. Thus saith the Lord; Though they be quiet, and likewise many, yet thus shall they be cut down, when he shall pass through. Though I have afflicted thee, I will afflict thee no more.

schools.summary: Ellicott pauses over how the clause about the one that comes out should be construed, noting a possible rendering that would make the man retire from Jerusalem rather than come out of Nineveh, and preferring the received version; at the next verse his rendering does most work, reading that though they be of unimpaired strength and ever so numerous, yet just in that state shall they be cut down, so that destruction comes upon the Assyrian army in the very hour of its prosperity. He also renders the close as a promise that God, having afflicted Jerusalem, will afflict her no more.

Gill takes the man to be either the king who had his royal seat there or the officer sent from him with a railing and blaspheming message to Jerusalem, and reads the quiet and numerous enemy of the besieging army rather than of the empire, as men secure before Jerusalem who feared no sally and betook themselves to sleep and rest; he applies the whole to the same deliverance, treating the passing through as the stroke by which the besiegers were removed. Calvin reaches Ellicott's sense by another road, that Nineveh promised itself a tranquil state because it was well fortified and wide in empire, and that this security is no impediment to the hand of God.

Clarke widens the reference to a succession of Assyrian invaders, listing four kings who imagined evil against the Lord before settling on the last of them and his spokesman as the wicked counsellor, and supplies the numbers, that the invasion was made with nearly two hundred thousand and that a hundred and eighty-five thousand were slain in a single night by what he describes as a suffocating wind. Wesley names the agent as the angel of the Lord, reads the cutting down as irresistible, sudden and universal, and makes the closing address direct, that God will no more use that rod upon Israel.

debates.question: Who is the one that comes out, and from where?

positions.position: Addressed to Nineveh; the received version is preferred over a rendering that would have the man retire from Jerusalem, and what follows identifies the enemy with Sennacherib.
Either the king who had his royal seat there or the officer sent from him with a blaspheming message to Jerusalem.
A succession of Assyrian invaders, four kings in all, before settling on the last and his spokesman.

debates.question: Of whom is the quiet and numerous enemy spoken?

positions.position: Of the empire in its unimpaired strength, cut down in the very hour of its prosperity.
Of the besieging army before Jerusalem, secure because so numerous, betaking themselves to sleep and rest.

outliers.claim: Supplies the numbers of the invasion, nearly two hundred thousand in the army and a hundred and eighty-five thousand slain in a single night, and attributes the slaughter to a suffocating wind.

themes: There is one come out of thee, that imagineth evil against the Lord, a wicked counsellor.
Thus saith the Lord; Though they be quiet, and likewise many, yet thus shall they be cut down, when he shall pass through. Though I have afflicted thee, I will afflict thee no more.

13.pericope_label: For now will I break his yoke from off thee, and will burst thy bonds in sunder. And the Lord hath given a commandment concerning thee, that no more of thy name be sown: out of the house of thy gods will I cut off the graven image and the molten image: I will make thy grave; for thou art vile. Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace! O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts, perform thy vows: for the wicked shall no more pass through thee; he is utterly cut off.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch render the sentence with the bursting of the bonds and carry straight on into the commandment given concerning the enemy. Ellicott sets beside the broken yoke the almost identical promise of an earlier prophet, that God would break the Assyrian in his land and tread him under foot on his mountain; he begins the next verse with a point of style, that sudden changes of person are a common feature of Hebrew poetry, and on that footing reads Sennacherib as told that the royal line is to be exterminated, a prediction he takes to have been accomplished when the last king of that city, his own great-grandson, destroyed himself in despair.

Gill identifies the yoke as the Assyrian yoke lifted from the Jews, who had paid tribute since the days of Ahaz and were in bondage while shut up and besieged, the country around laid under contribution, and who were delivered when that army was destroyed; he localises the mountains of the last verse, following the Targum, as those of the land of Israel or the hills about Jerusalem. Calvin uses that verse to state what the whole prophecy was for, that God might show by so remarkable an evidence that he had a care for his people and was not unmindful of the covenant made with the children of Abraham.

Clarke names the tribute specifically as what the yoke means, and observes that the language of the messenger on the mountains is probably borrowed from an earlier prophet and applied here to those who brought the good tidings of Nineveh's destruction, after which Judah might keep her solemn feasts because the oppressor would pass through the land no more. Wesley reads the address about the name as taking effect in the place where the king died, the house of his gods being his grave, and reads the two closing commands as one, that they should serve God and perform the vows made in their distress.

debates.question: What is the yoke that is broken?

positions.position: The Assyrian yoke on the Jews since the days of Ahaz, with tribute, siege and the country laid under contribution, lifted when the army was destroyed.
The tribute specifically.
Read against the earlier prophet's promise that the Assyrian would be broken in God's land and the yoke depart from off them.

debates.question: How is the threat against the name to be understood?

positions.position: As a sentence on the royal line, exterminated when the last king of the city destroyed himself in despair.
As fulfilled in the manner of the king's death, the house of his gods being made his grave while he worshipped there.

outliers.claim: Without the closing promise the prophecy would have produced no wholesome effect at all, since the people might have supposed that the overthrow of Nineveh came about by chance, or by some revolution of fortune, or through some other cause.

themes: For now will I break his yoke from off thee, and will burst thy bonds in sunder.

And the Lord hath given a commandment concerning thee, that no more of thy name be sown: out of the house of thy gods will I cut off the graven image and the molten image: I will make thy grave; for thou art vile.

Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace! O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts, perform thy vows: for the wicked shall no more pass through thee; he is utterly cut off.
